# About me

I'm Abdullah, a final-year Computer Science student at the University of Management and Technology (UMT). My main interests are deep learning research and cybersecurity, and I also like building complete AI products from the database all the way up to the API.

On the research side, I'm drawn to security applications of machine learning: intrusion detection systems, phishing detection, adversarial machine learning, and federated learning. I've also explored multi-agent LLM security and attacks on the memory and planner components of LLM agents.

On the product side, I co-own Resona, an AI research platform. I handle the whole backend, the machine learning parts and the infrastructure, while my partner Sharina handles the frontend.

I also take freelance work on Fiverr, mostly text classification and email classification projects.

My long-term goal is to do deep learning research and eventually build a significant AI venture. I want to be the kind of person who can both read the papers and ship the system.

## How my days usually look

I'm an early riser, usually awake between 4:00 and 4:30 AM. I like structured days built around blocks of deep work, and I go to the gym in the evening, around 9:30 to 10:30 PM.

## Music

I enjoy hip hop.

# CODEAN: my final year project

CODEAN is my final year project at UMT, done as a team of three, with Dr. Muhammad Wasim as supervisor (session 2026-2027). It's an MCP-based autonomous software engineering system. In plain words: it sits next to an AI coding assistant and makes that assistant cheaper, better informed and safer.

## The problem
AI coding tools burn a lot of tokens reading code they don't need, they hallucinate APIs that don't exist or have changed, and they sometimes suggest packages that don't exist, which attackers can register with malware (this is called slopsquatting).

## The idea
CODEAN is one closed-loop pipeline, not separate modules:
1. Structural exploration: Tree-Sitter builds an AST knowledge graph of the codebase.
2. Context pruning: a dual-rubric method keeps only the code relevant to the task, which saves tokens.
3. API grounding: Context7 provides live, versioned documentation, so the model doesn't rely on stale memory.
4. Deterministic verification: runtime introspection and deterministic AST rewriting check and auto-repair the generated code.
5. Package screening: OSV.dev, PyPI and npm lookups plus a Random Forest classifier flag suspicious or slopsquatted packages.

## Architecture and delivery
It ships as a local MCP server that works with VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf and Claude Code. # Study notes: backend engineering

I handle backend and infrastructure for Resona, so these are my working notes on the stack I use.

## Async FastAPI
FastAPI is a Python web framework built on Starlette and Pydantic. Handlers can be declared with async def so the event loop can serve other requests while one request waits on the database or a network call. This matters for I/O-heavy apps such as search and chat features. Pydantic models validate request and response data and generate OpenAPI documentation automatically. A blocking call inside an async handler, such as a synchronous database driver or a heavy computation, stalls the event loop, so CPU-heavy work belongs in a background worker.

## SQLAlchemy and asyncpg
SQLAlchemy is the ORM and query toolkit, and asyncpg is a fast asynchronous PostgreSQL driver. Together they allow async sessions that do not block the event loop. Good practice is one session per request, explicit transactions, and migrations managed with a tool such as Alembic.

## PostgreSQL schema design
Resona's schema has 30 tables grouped into 11 modules. Grouping tables into modules (for example users, papers, collaboration, messaging) keeps responsibilities clear. Foreign keys enforce integrity, indexes speed up common queries, and normalization avoids duplicated data. For text search and embeddings, PostgreSQL can hold both relational data and vectors in the same database through the pgvector extension.

## Background jobs with Celery and Redis
Slow work, such as parsing a PDF, generating embeddings or calling an LLM for a long document, should not block a web request. Celery workers pull tasks from a queue, with Redis acting as the broker and sometimes the result backend. The API returns quickly with a task ID, and the client polls or is notified when the job finishes. Retries, time limits and idempotent tasks make failures easier to handle.

## Nginx and TLS
Nginx works as a reverse proxy in front of the application server, handling TLS termination, compression and routing. Certbot can issue and renew free Let's Encrypt certificates. Although I am not deploying Resona publicly for now, I designed the stack with a VPS deployment on Nginx in mind.

## Authentication
JWT-based authentication issues a signed token after login, which the client sends with each request. Tokens should have short lifetimes, secrets must be kept out of the repository, and passwords must be stored hashed. In Veritas I supported Google OAuth as well as email and password sign-in. In CCDA I used SHA-256 hashed tokens for email verification.

## Tooling habits
I use uv for Python dependency management (`uv add`, never pip install) because it is fast and keeps the lockfile consistent. I run PostgreSQL 17 with pgvector and pgAdmin in Docker so the database setup is reproducible and does not depend on the Ubuntu system packages. ## Local LLMs
My laptop has no discrete GPU, so I run small models on CPU using Ollama, with Open WebUI as the interface. Quantized models make this practical, trading a little quality for a lot less memory.

## Automation with n8n
For my internship I built a Multi-channel AI Agent in n8n. In Phase 1, three channels (website chat, email and a simulated WhatsApp) all enter the system through webhooks and flow into one central AI agent that uses Mistral as the language model. Messages are stored in Google Sheets in Phase 1, and the design leaves room for a real database later. The point of the architecture is that every channel is normalized into one message format, so the agent logic is written once.

# Study notes: machine learning pipelines from my projects

## Text classification baselines
For text classification, including my Fiverr work, I start with a classical baseline. TF-IDF turns text into sparse weighted word-count vectors, and a linear model such as logistic regression or a linear SVM is trained on top. It is fast, cheap and often surprisingly hard to beat on small datasets. Only after the baseline do I consider fine-tuning a transformer, since the gain has to justify the extra cost.

## Stylometric features
Stylometry measures writing style instead of topic: sentence length, punctuation habits, vocabulary richness, function-word frequencies. In my Urdu fake news detector I combined TF-IDF with stylometric features, because fake and real articles often differ in style as well as content.

## Fine-tuning transformers
XLM-RoBERTa is a multilingual transformer pretrained on text in around a hundred languages, which makes it a good choice for Urdu. Fine-tuning adds a classification head and updates the model weights on labeled data. I trained on a Kaggle TPU v5e-8 using a cleaned dataset of 62,017 rows. Important practices are a proper train/validation/test split, a small learning rate, watching for overfitting, and comparing against the TF-IDF baseline.

## Gradient boosting and explainability
In CCDA I used LightGBM, a gradient boosting library that builds trees sequentially, each correcting the errors of the previous ones. To explain predictions I used SHAP, which assigns each feature a contribution to an individual prediction, based on Shapley values from game theory. This lets a user see why the model rated a trade deal the way it did.

## Target leakage
When CCDA showed 100 percent accuracy, that was a warning sign and not a success. Target leakage happens when a feature contains information that would not be available at prediction time, or is derived from the label itself, so the model effectively sees the answer. The fix is to audit features, make sure the split respects time or groups, and be suspicious of any result that looks too perfect.

## Object detection and sequence recognition
My CAPTCHA breaker used two models. Faster R-CNN is a two-stage object detector: a region proposal network suggests candidate boxes and a second stage classifies and refines them. I used it for CAPTCHAs made of geometric shapes. For distorted words I used a CRNN, a convolutional network that extracts visual features feeding a recurrent network, trained with CTC loss. CTC lets the model learn to read a sequence of characters without needing per-character alignment between the image and the label. I trained both on Kaggle GPUs and served them locally through FastAPI.

## Dataset building for a humanizer model
For the text humanizer feature planned for Resona, the dataset plan is to start from human-written academic text from S2ORC or peS2o, beginning with computer science sections, then generate AI-like versions of each paragraph so that human and AI pairs exist. The data is stored in JSONL, the model to fine-tune is Qwen3-8B, and the first version targets about 5,000 paragraphs, scaling to 20,000 to 50,000 later. The scope of the tool is language-level editing only: grammar, AI-sounding phrasing and flow. It does not change the logic or arguments.

I try to keep a held-out test set untouched until the end, report more than accuracy when classes are imbalanced (precision, recall, F1), compare against a simple baseline, and check explanations with SHAP or error analysis. ## Search and hybrid retrieval in practice
Veritas ingests news from GNews and NewsAPI every six hours using Celery and Redis. Articles are embedded and stored with pgvector. A query goes through BM25 and dense retrieval, the two ranked lists are fused with RRF, and a cross-encoder reranks the top results. A personalized For You feed uses stored user signals. # Study notes: retrieval and RAG

These are my notes on how retrieval-augmented generation works, based on what I built in Veritas and Resona and on my NLP course preparation.

## The RAG pipeline in four steps
RAG exists because a language model only knows what was in its training data and it can hallucinate. Instead of trusting its memory, we fetch relevant text first and make the model answer from that text.
1. Chunk: split documents into passages, usually a few hundred words, with a small overlap so a sentence at a boundary is not lost. Each chunk keeps metadata such as the source file and an ID.
2. Index: build a searchable representation of every chunk. This can be a keyword index, an embedding index, or both.
3. Retrieve: for each question, rank the chunks by relevance and keep the top k.
4. Generate: put the top chunks and the question into the prompt, and instruct the model to answer only from that context and to admit when the context does not contain the answer.

The quality of the final answer is capped by retrieval. If the right chunk is not in the top k, the model cannot use it, and a good model will either guess or say it does not know.

## Chunking decisions
Chunks that are too small lose context, so a pronoun or a heading ends up separated from what it refers to. Chunks that are too large dilute the embedding, because one vector has to summarize many topics, and they waste prompt space. A range of about 200 to 300 words with an overlap of roughly 10 to 15 percent is a sensible default. Splitting on paragraph boundaries is better than cutting blindly by word count, because a question and its answer in a FAQ should stay in the same chunk.

## BM25: keyword retrieval
BM25 is a ranking function from the family of TF-IDF methods. For each query term it scores a document using three ideas:
- Term frequency: more occurrences of the term in the chunk means a higher score, but with diminishing returns (saturation), so repeating a word ten times does not make a chunk ten times better.
- Inverse document frequency: rare terms matter more than common ones. A project name that appears in one chunk is a strong signal, while the word "the" tells you nothing.
- Length normalization: long chunks are penalized so they do not win just by containing more words.

Strengths: it is exact, fast, needs no model, and is excellent when the question contains a rare specific term such as a project name, a tool or a place. Weakness: it only matches tokens. If the question says "How do you relax?" and the answer says "I go cycling in the evening," there is no shared word, so BM25 scores zero. It also does not understand synonyms or paraphrases. Preprocessing such as lowercasing and removing stopwords helps, and a score of zero should be treated as no match instead of ranking zero-score chunks arbitrarily.

## Dense retrieval with sentence embeddings
A sentence-embedding model such as all-MiniLM-L6-v2 maps each chunk to a vector, 384 dimensions in that case, so that texts with similar meaning land close together. The question is embedded the same way and compared to every chunk vector using cosine similarity. If the vectors are normalized to unit length, cosine similarity is just a dot product, which numpy handles quickly for a small corpus. Embeddings for the chunks only need to be computed once and can be saved to disk, for example as a .npy file, then loaded at startup.

Strengths: it handles paraphrases, synonyms and loosely worded questions. Weakness: it can miss exact rare terms, because a rare name may be poorly represented in the embedding model's vocabulary, and it can return chunks that are topically similar but do not actually contain the answer. Similarity scores also have no built-in meaning of "good enough," so a threshold has to be tuned.

## Why two methods fail differently
BM25 fails when wording differs and succeeds on exact terms. Dense retrieval fails on rare exact terms and succeeds when meaning matches without shared words. Because their errors are different, combining them is useful. This is the main motivation for hybrid search, and the BEIR benchmark showed that BM25 is a surprisingly strong baseline outside the domain a dense model was trained on.

## Hybrid fusion
Two rankings can be merged in two common ways.
- Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF): the score of a chunk is the sum over rankings of 1 / (k + rank), with k usually 60. It only uses ranks, so there is no need to normalize scores that live on different scales, BM25 scores being unbounded and cosine scores being between -1 and 1. A chunk that appears high in both lists gets the highest fused score. I used RRF in Veritas.
- Weighted score fusion: normalize each score list with min-max scaling and combine them as alpha times the dense score plus (1 minus alpha) times the BM25 score. This gives a tunable knob but depends on good normalization and a well-chosen alpha.

## Reranking
Retrieval models such as BM25 and bi-encoders score the query and the chunk independently. A cross-encoder reads the query and the chunk together in one pass, which is slower but more accurate. A common pattern is to retrieve a few dozen candidates cheaply, then rerank them with a cross-encoder such as ms-marco-MiniLM, and send only the best few to the language model. Veritas used this pattern.

## Evaluating retrieval
Common measures in information retrieval are precision (how many retrieved items are relevant), recall (how many relevant items were found), hit@k (whether a correct chunk appears in the top k), and mean reciprocal rank. A small hand-labeled set of questions with the correct chunk for each is enough to compare BM25, dense and hybrid on hit@3.

## Grounded generation
A good RAG prompt does four things: it sets a persona, it tells the model to answer only from the supplied context, it gives an explicit fallback sentence for missing information, and it tells the model to treat the context as data, not instructions. Honest behavior matters more than fluency, because an invented answer is worse than "I don't have that."

## pgvector
In Resona and Veritas I store embeddings in PostgreSQL using the pgvector extension, so semantic search lives in the same database as the rest of the application data. It supports cosine, inner product and L2 distance, and approximate indexes such as HNSW for fast nearest-neighbor search on larger collections. Resona's novelty-checking idea used cosine similarity over section-level embeddings, though I dropped that feature from version one.

# Study notes: machine learning for security

My main research interest is deep learning applied to cybersecurity. These notes summarize the areas I have worked on or explored.

## Intrusion detection systems
An intrusion detection system (IDS) monitors network traffic or host activity and flags malicious behavior. There are two classic approaches. Signature-based detection matches known attack patterns, which is precise but blind to new attacks. Anomaly-based detection learns what normal traffic looks like and flags deviations, which can catch novel attacks but produces more false positives. Machine learning IDS work typically uses flow features such as packet counts, byte counts, durations, flags and ports, and trains classifiers on labeled datasets. The main practical difficulties are class imbalance, because attacks are rare, dataset age and realism, and keeping false positive rates low enough for a human analyst to trust the alerts. I built an AI-powered IDS earlier as a project.

## Phishing detection
Phishing detection can look at the email text, the headers, the URLs and the sender. Text models classify language that creates urgency or asks for credentials. URL features include length, number of subdomains, use of IP addresses, and look-alike domains. I built an email phishing detector with a Chrome extension, so detection could happen in the browser as the user reads a message.

## Adversarial machine learning
Models can be attacked in several ways. Evasion attacks change an input slightly at inference time so the model misclassifies it, a famous example being imperceptible noise on an image. Poisoning attacks corrupt the training data so the model learns something wrong or contains a hidden backdoor. Model extraction and membership inference attacks try to steal the model or learn whether a record was in the training set. Defenses include adversarial training, input validation, and monitoring. This area interests me because it asks how much a model can be trusted when someone is actively trying to fool it.

## Federated learning
In federated learning, many clients train a model on their own local data and only share model updates with a central server, which aggregates them, for example with federated averaging. Raw data never leaves the client, which helps privacy. It is useful in security because organizations often cannot share network logs with each other. Challenges include non-identical data across clients, communication cost, and the fact that updates themselves can still leak information or be poisoned by a malicious client.

## Security of LLM agents
LLM agents use tools, planners and memory. That creates new attack surfaces: prompt injection through retrieved documents or web pages, poisoning of the memory an agent reads later, manipulating the planner so it chooses harmful tool calls, and abusing tool permissions. I explored research directions on multi-agent LLM security, including an intrusion detection proposal for multi-agent systems (MA-LLM-IDS) with Sharina, adversarial attacks on the memory and planner parts of agents, and agentic malware detection frameworks.

## Slopsquatting and supply-chain risk
AI coding assistants sometimes suggest package names that do not exist, a kind of hallucination. Attackers can register those names on registries like PyPI or npm and put malware in them, hoping developers install what the assistant suggested. This is called slopsquatting. In CODEAN, the package screening stage checks candidate packages against OSV.dev vulnerability data and the PyPI and npm registries, and uses a Random Forest classifier over features such as package age, download counts and metadata to flag suspicious ones.

## Digital forensics
For my cyber forensics course I used Autopsy to examine disk images and ExifTool to read metadata. Metadata such as camera model, timestamps and GPS coordinates inside images, documents and media files can reveal when and where a file was created or changed. Forensic work needs a careful workflow: keep originals untouched, work on copies, and produce reports of what was found.

# My preferences, principles and trade-offs

This document collects how I tend to make decisions, based on choices I've actually made. It is not a list of hot takes.

## How I like to build
I like owning a system end to end. On Resona I take the entire backend, the ML and the infrastructure, because I want to understand how a product fits together from the database schema to the API. My default stack is async FastAPI, PostgreSQL with pgvector and Linux, and I've stayed with it across projects instead of switching tools for novelty. I keep embeddings next to the rest of my application data in PostgreSQL, so semantic search doesn't need a separate system.

## Tool habits
I always use uv for Python packages and never pip install. I run PostgreSQL 17 with pgvector and pgAdmin in Docker when the system packages lag behind, which keeps my setup reproducible. I like dark themes: Brave in dark mode with a tiles-only new tab page, and I'm building a custom dark-tile new tab extension for it. I'm also curious about running models locally, so I use Ollama and Open WebUI on a CPU-only laptop and keep LM Studio installed as an alternative.

## Scoping and product decisions
I'm willing to cut features to ship something real. In Resona version one I removed the AI Novelty Checker because I wasn't convinced it was useful, and the Citation Generator because there wasn't time. I chose not to deploy Resona publicly yet and not to open-source it. I also kept delaying Resona in the past because of university projects, hackathons and extra courses, so I now try to make it part of work I'm already doing.

## Architecture decisions
For CODEAN I first planned Python and TypeScript only, then changed my mind: Rust for the heavy compute and indexing engine, Python for the MCP server layer, and TypeScript with React for the visualization UI. I use existing projects such as codebase-memory-mcp as architecture references only, and I don't want to clone them.

## On AI writing tools
For my text humanizer idea I want a whole-document workflow, not paragraph-by-paragraph pasting. The tool should read the full document, fix language problems and AI-sounding phrasing, and return something ready to use. It should only correct, not write, and it must not alter the researcher's logic or arguments, because I think that is the author's own responsibility.

## On results and skepticism
A perfect accuracy score makes me suspicious. When CCDA showed 100 percent, the likely explanation was target leakage, so I audit features and splits before believing a result.

## How I like feedback
I prefer being challenged over being agreed with: counterpoints, tested logic and alternative perspectives are more useful to me than praise, and I would rather hear the truth.

## Routine and downtime
I'm an early riser, usually up between 4:00 and 4:30 AM, and I plan my days around deep work blocks. I go to the gym in the evening, and I enjoy hip hop.

## Goals and values
I want to do deep learning research and eventually build a significant AI venture. I value being able to both understand the research and ship the system.

# Other projects I've built

**Veritas** is a news search engine I built for my NLP course. The backend is FastAPI with PostgreSQL and pgvector, the frontend is Next.js, and Celery with Redis ingests news from GNews and NewsAPI every six hours. Search uses hybrid retrieval: BM25 plus dense embeddings fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, then reranked with a cross-encoder (ms-marco-MiniLM). It has JWT auth with Google OAuth, and a personalized "For You" feed. I defended it in the course viva.

**FocusOS** is an HCI course project I built with Sharina: an AI deep work platform for enterprise teams. It uses Next.js 14, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Mistral AI and Tesseract OCR, and the design is grounded in Flow Theory, Cognitive Load Theory, user-centered design, and the SUS and NASA-TLX evaluation scales.

**CCDA (CrossCountry Deal Advisor)** is a capstone-style project that predicts and explains trade deals using LightGBM and SHAP, with data from the World Bank, IMF and UN Comtrade, plus a RAG chat assistant on pgvector. When I first saw a suspiciously perfect accuracy, I learned to suspect target leakage instead of celebrating.

**Urdu fake news detection:** a pipeline combining TF-IDF and stylometric features with a fine-tuned XLM-RoBERTa, trained on a Kaggle TPU v5e-8 over a cleaned dataset of 62,017 rows.

**CAPTCHA breaker:** Faster R-CNN for geometric-shape CAPTCHAs and a CRNN with CTC loss for distorted-word CAPTCHAs, trained on Kaggle GPUs and served locally through FastAPI.

# Resona: my AI research platform

Resona is an AI research SaaS that I co-own with my partner Sharina. She builds the Next.js frontend, and I own the entire backend, the machine learning and the infrastructure. It competes with tools like Perplexity, Elicit and SciSpace, and the idea is to put the whole research workflow for a student or researcher in one place instead of five different tabs.

## What it does
Resona has AI Search, Discover, History, a Literature Review tool, a Paper Writer, an AI Paraphraser, a Dataset Finder, Chat with PDF, an AI Content Detector, and a Collaborate area with three privacy levels: Public, Signal Mode and Private. It also has a social network and messaging so researchers can talk to each other. I'm also working on a text humanizer feature that fixes grammar and AI-sounding phrasing across a whole document. It only edits the language, and never writes new content or touches the argument, because that stays the researcher's job.

## How I built the backend
The backend is async FastAPI with SQLAlchemy and asyncpg on top of PostgreSQL. I use the pgvector extension for embeddings and semantic similarity search. Redis and Celery handle background jobs such as processing papers, and Nginx sits in front. The database schema has 30 tables grouped into 11 modules. Retrieval-augmented generation powers the features that need answers grounded in real papers.

## Decisions I made
For version one I cut the AI Novelty Checker, because I wasn't sure it was a useful feature, and the Citation Generator, because it was out of scope for the time I had. I'm not deploying Resona publicly for now, so it runs locally. I'm also not open-sourcing the product. For payments, I looked at Paddle and Dodo Payments because Stripe doesn't support Pakistani merchant accounts.

## Why I'm building it
Resona is my attempt to turn research skills into a real product. It's where I practice database design, retrieval, infrastructure and product thinking together.
